items.zh: 云何瑜伽師地？謂十七地。何等十七？嗢拕南曰：五識相應、意、有尋伺等三、三摩地俱、非、有心、無心地、聞、思、修所立、如是具三乘、有依、及無依，是名十七地。一者、五識身相應地，二者、意地，三者、有尋有伺地，四者、無尋唯伺地，五者、無尋無伺地，六者、三摩呬多地，七者、非三摩呬多地，八者、有心地，九者、無心地，十者、聞所成地，十一者、思所成地，十二者、修所成地，十三者、聲聞地，十四者、獨覺地，十五者、菩薩地，十六者、有餘依地，十七者、無餘依地。如是略說十七，名為瑜伽師地。
云何五識身相應地？
items.en: What is the Stage Corresponding to the Body of the Five Sense Consciousnesses?

items.zh: 謂五識身自性，彼所依，彼所緣，彼助伴，彼作業，如是總名五識身相應地。
items.en: It is the self-nature of the body of the five sense consciousnesses, their support, their object, their accompaniments, and their activity. Taken together, these are named the Stage Corresponding to the Body of the Five Sense Consciousnesses.

items.zh: 何等名為五識身耶？所謂眼識、耳識、鼻識、舌識、身識。
items.en: What are the body of the five sense consciousnesses? They are: the eye-consciousness, the ear-consciousness, the nose-consciousness, the tongue-consciousness, and the body-consciousness.

items.zh: 云何眼識自性？謂依眼，了別色。
items.en: What is the self-nature of the eye-consciousness? It is the discerning of colour-form in dependence on the eye.

items.zh: 彼所依者，俱有依，謂眼。
items.en: Its support: the co-existent support is the eye.

items.zh: 等無間依，謂意。
items.en: The immediately-preceding support is the manas.

items.zh: 種子依，謂即此一切種子執受所依異熟所攝阿賴耶識。
items.en: The seed support is the ālayavijñāna — the ripening consciousness that holds and carries all seeds.

items.zh: 如是略說二種所依。謂色、非色。
items.en: Such, briefly stated, are two kinds of support: the form-kind and the non-form-kind.

items.zh: 眼是色，餘非色。
items.en: The eye is form; the rest are non-form.

items.zh: 眼，謂四大種所造眼識所依淨色，無見有對。
items.en: The eye is the pure form, made of the four great elements, on which the eye-consciousness depends — invisible, yet with obstruction.

items.zh: 意，謂眼識無間過去識。
items.en: The manas is the eye-consciousness's own immediately-past moment.

items.zh: 一切種子識，謂無始時來樂著戲論熏習為因所生一切種子異熟識。
items.en: The all-seeds consciousness is the ripened-effect consciousness holding all seeds, produced from the beginningless perfuming of delight in elaboration as its cause.

items.zh: 彼所緣者，謂色，有見有對。此復多種。略說有三，謂顯色、形色、表色。
items.en: Its object is form — visible, and with obstruction. This again has many kinds. Briefly stated, there are three: visible colour, shape, and expressive form.

items.zh: 顯色者，謂青、黃、赤、白、光、影、明、闇、雲、煙、塵、霧，及空一顯色。
items.en: Visible colour is: blue, yellow, red, and white; light, shadow, brightness, and darkness; cloud, smoke, dust, and mist; and the single visible colour of open sky.

items.zh: 形色者，謂長、短、方、圓、麁、細、正、不正、高、下色。
items.en: Shape is: long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, regular, irregular, high, and low.

items.zh: 表色者，謂取、捨、屈、伸、行、住、坐、臥，如是等色。
items.en: Expressive form is: taking, releasing, bending, stretching, walking, standing, sitting, and lying — forms of this kind.

items.zh: 又顯色者，謂若色顯了，眼識所行。形色者，謂若色積集長短等分別相。表色者，謂即此積集色，生滅相續，由變異因，於先生處不復重生，轉於異處，或無間、或有間、或近、或遠差別生。或即於此處變異生，是名表色。又顯色者，謂光、明等差別。形色者，謂長、短等積集差別。表色者，謂業用為依轉動差別。如是一切顯、形、表色，是眼所行、眼境界、眼識所行、眼識境界、眼識所緣，意識所行、意識境界、意識所緣，名之差別。又即此色復有三種。謂若好顯色、若惡顯色、若俱異顯色，似色顯現。
彼助伴者，謂彼俱有相應諸心所有法。所謂作意、觸、受、想、思、及餘眼識俱有相應諸心所有法。
items.en: Its accompaniments are the mental factors that co-arise and correspond with it — namely attention, contact, feeling, perception, and volition, together with whatever other mental factors correspond and co-arise with the eye-consciousness.

items.zh: 又彼諸法同一所緣，非一行相，俱有相應，一一而轉。
items.en: These, moreover, all take the same object, yet not the same aspect; they co-arise and correspond, each operating in its own particular way.

items.zh: 又彼一切各各從自種子而生。
items.en: And each of these, in every case, arises from its own seed.

items.zh: 彼作業者，當知有六種。謂唯了別自境所緣，是名初業。
items.en: Its activity should be understood as sixfold. The first is: it discerns only its own object — this is called the first activity.

items.zh: 唯了別自相，唯了別現在，唯一剎那了別。
items.en: It discerns only the particular mark [of its object, not the mark it shares with other things]; it discerns only the present; and it discerns for only a single moment.

items.zh: 復有二業。謂隨意識轉、隨善染轉、隨發業轉。
items.en: There are, further, two more activities. [The first of these is:] it follows the mental consciousness's turning, follows its turning towards the wholesome or the defiled, and follows its turning towards the initiating of action.

items.zh: 又復能取愛非愛果，是第六業。
items.en: And it is, further, able to bring about a desirable or an undesirable result — this is the sixth activity.

items.zh: 云何耳識自性？謂依耳，了別聲。彼所依者，俱有依，謂耳。等無間依，謂意。種子依，謂一切種子阿賴耶識。耳，謂四大種所造耳識所依淨色，無見有對。
items.en: What is the self-nature of the ear-consciousness? It is the discerning of sound in dependence on the ear. Its support: the co-existent support is the ear; the immediately-preceding support is the manas; the seed support is the all-seeds ālayavijñāna. The ear is the pure form, made of the four great elements, on which the ear-consciousness depends — invisible, yet with obstruction.

items.zh: 意及種子，如前分別。
彼所緣者，謂聲，無見有對。此復多種。如螺貝聲、大小鼓聲、舞聲、歌聲、諸音樂聲、俳戲叫聲、女聲、男聲、風林等聲、明了聲、不明了聲、有義聲、無義聲、下中上聲、江河等聲、鬪諍諠雜聲、受持演說聲、論義決擇聲。如是等類，有眾多聲。
items.en: Its object is sound — invisible, yet with obstruction. This again has many kinds: the sound of a conch-shell; the sound of large and small drums; the sound of dancing; the sound of singing; the sounds of music of every kind; the cry of theatrical performance; a woman's voice; a man's voice; the sound of wind and of forests and such things; clear sound and unclear sound; meaningful sound and meaningless sound; low, middling, and high sound; the sound of rivers and such things; the clamour of quarreling and disputing; the sound of reciting and expounding the teaching; the sound of debate and analytical inquiry. Sounds of this and other such kinds are many.

items.zh: 此略三種。謂因執受大種聲、因不執受大種聲、因執受不執受大種聲。初唯內緣聲，次唯外緣聲，後內外緣聲。此復三種。謂可意聲、不可意聲、俱相違聲。
items.en: Briefly, there are three kinds: sound caused by appropriated great elements, sound caused by non-appropriated great elements, and sound caused by both together. The first arises purely from within; the second purely from without; the third from within and without together. This, again, is threefold: agreeable sound, disagreeable sound, and sound that is neither.

items.zh: 又復聲者，謂鳴、音、詞、吼表彰語等差別之名。是耳所行、耳境界，耳識所行、耳識境界、耳識所緣，意識所行、意識境界、意識所緣。助伴及業，如眼識應知。
items.en: Sound, again, has these further names: cry, tone, utterance, roar, and expressive speech, among other such distinctions. It is what the ear operates on, the ear's realm; what the ear-consciousness operates on, its realm, and its object; and what the mental consciousness operates on, its realm, and its object. Its accompaniments and activity should be understood as with the eye-consciousness.

blocks.text: Today we begin the treatise itself. It opens by naming the seventeen stages (十七地), then begins the first of them, the **Stage Corresponding to the Body of the Five Sense Consciousnesses** (五識身相應地). The eye-consciousness is explained in full under five headings: self-nature, support, object, accompaniments, and activity. The ear-consciousness is then explained on the same pattern, more briefly. Watch the five headings: they will be applied to all five sense consciousnesses, and then to the mind.

Two passages today are not yet in Ru-Yi's translation: the opening list of the seventeen stages (0279a08–a21) and the second and third explanations of visible colour, shape, and expressive form (0279b08–b19). The Chinese is given in full and the English column is marked. The commentary below summarises what they say.

subs.head: "What are the stages of the yoga practitioner?"

blocks.text: The treatise begins with a short question and a short answer ("the seventeen stages"), then a longer question ("which seventeen?") and a longer answer, first in verse and then in prose. Master Cháng Bǎi notes that this pattern of brief question, brief answer, full question, full answer runs through the whole work.

The verse is an **uddāna** (嗢拕南), which the *Pīxún jì* glosses as "gathering and giving" (集施): a few words gather many dharmas and give them to students in a form they can hold. The whole of the Basic Section is packed into forty characters. Master Cháng Bǎi recommends doing the same with our own study: reduce a passage to a few key words, and the rest will come back when needed. (The seventeen are listed in Introduction 2.)

The first stage is defined by five items: the consciousnesses' **self-nature** (自性, *svabhāva*), **support** (所依, *āśraya*), **object** (所緣, *ālambana*), **accompaniments** (助伴, *sahāya*), and **activity** (作業, *karman*). Master Cháng Bǎi, following the *Pīxún jì*, explains "corresponding" (相應) as these five being present together and operating together. Venerable Miào Jìng puts it in human terms: the five "accord with one another" and do one job together, like people who get along.

Master Cháng Bǎi draws a contrast that will matter later. A real mental event has a self-nature, a support, an object, and so on. Merely nominal dharmas, such as birth, ageing, or impermanence, are labels laid over physical and mental events; they have no support or object of their own. These are the **formations dissociated from mind** (心不相應行法), twenty-four in all, and they are "not corresponding" for exactly this reason.

subs.head: Self-nature: discerning, in dependence on the eye

blocks.text: All eight consciousnesses **discern** (了別, *vijñapti*). What makes this one the *eye*-consciousness is that it depends on the eye and discerns colour-form. The *Pīxún jì*: it is called "eye" because the eye is its support, and "consciousness" because it discerns form.
The eye-consciousness needs three supports. Both teachers map them onto the classical **four conditions** (四緣):

items: The **co-existent support** (俱有依) is the eye-faculty. It exists at the same moment as the eye-consciousness, and if it is damaged the consciousness suffers with it. This is the **dominant condition** (增上緣, *adhipati-pratyaya*).

The **immediately-preceding support** (等無間依), here called *manas* (意), is the moment of eye-consciousness that has just ceased. By ceasing, it "opens the way" for the next moment, with nothing in between. This is the **immediately-preceding condition** (等無間緣, *samanantara-pratyaya*). The *Cheng Weishi Lun* calls it the "opening-and-leading support" (開導依).
The **seed support** (種子依) is the ālayavijñāna, which holds the seed of eye-consciousness. This is the **causal condition** (因緣, *hetu-pratyaya*) proper.

blocks.text: The fourth condition, the **object condition** (所緣緣), is the visible form described below.

A warning, which both teachers give: the *manas* here is **not** the seventh consciousness. Venerable Miào Jìng: "This 意 is not the 意 of the sixth consciousness … here it means support." The treatise defines it itself (0279b01): the eye-consciousness's own immediately-past moment. On Day 3 the same word will be used in a second sense.

The eye-faculty is **pure form** (淨色, *rūpa-prasāda*): a subtle matter made of the four great elements, distinct from the visible eyeball, which the commentaries call the "supporting organ" (扶根塵). It is "invisible, yet with obstruction" (無見有對): it cannot be seen with the ordinary eye, but it occupies space and can be damaged.

subs.head: The all-seeds consciousness and "delight in elaboration"

blocks.text: The seed support is the ālayavijñāna as **all-seeds consciousness** (一切種子識), produced by "the beginningless perfuming of delight in elaboration". **Elaboration** (戲論, *prapañca*) is, at root, grasping at a self and at things as real. Master Cháng Bǎi lists the six kinds of elaboration given later in the treatise (fascicle 95): inverted talk, pointless talk, quarrelsome talk, comparing oneself with others, talk of trades and livelihoods, and talk of wealth and food. "If one has not learned the Dharma," he says, "life is elaboration and nothing but elaboration." Each act of this kind perfumes a seed.

Venerable Miào Jìng's image for **perfuming** (熏習, *vāsanā*) is incense placed in a wooden chest: nothing visible changes, yet the scent is fully there and will come out later. He adds that only what arises and ceases can be perfumed, so Yogācāra does not accept the *Awakening of Faith*'s idea of "suchness receiving perfuming".

The word **ripened** (異熟, *vipāka*) also appears here. The ālayavijñāna is the ripened result of past karma, ripening "at a different time, in a different way, in a different kind" from the acts that caused it.

subs.head: The object: colour, shape, and expressive form

blocks.text: Visible form is sorted three ways. **Visible colour** (顯色): the four basic colours, blue, yellow, red, and white, plus their variants, light, shadow, and so on. **Shape** (形色): long, short, square, round, and so on. **Expressive form** (表色): taking, releasing, bending, stretching, walking, standing, sitting, lying.

The untranslated passage (0279b08–b19) gives two more explanations of the same three. Visible colour is "what is clearly manifest" to the eye-consciousness. Shape is the discrimination of long and short in an accumulation of colour; the commentaries stress that shape is therefore only nominal (假色), set up by comparison: 171 centimetres is tall beside 160 and short beside 175. Expressive form is the same accumulation of colour arising moment by moment in a new place, driven by a "cause of change", which Master Cháng Bǎi identifies as the mental factor of volition (思). That is why a posture can express a state of mind.

The passage closes with three kinds of colour, pleasing, displeasing, and neither, which "appear as if form" (似色顯現). Master Cháng Bǎi takes this phrase as an early hint of consciousness-only: the same woman is seen by her son with reverence and by a stranger with desire. The pleasing or displeasing quality is supplied by the mind.

The eye-consciousness never arises alone. It is accompanied by **mental factors** (心所, *caitasika*), at least the five **universal factors** (遍行): **attention** (作意, *manaskāra*), **contact** (觸, *sparśa*), **feeling** (受, *vedanā*), **perception** (想, *saṃjñā*), and **volition** (思, *cetanā*). Mind and factors are like a king and his ministers. They share one object but each has its own aspect (行相, *ākāra*): consciousness grasps the object as a whole, feeling experiences it as pleasant or unpleasant, perception grasps its marks, and so on. Each arises from its own seed.

The eye-consciousness discerns only its own object, only the **particular mark** (自相, *svalakṣaṇa*), only the present, and only for a single moment. It cannot know that a flower is impermanent; that is a **shared mark** (共相, *sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), known by the mental consciousness. It also follows the mental consciousness into wholesome or defiled states and into action, and so it shares in bringing about pleasant or unpleasant results. Venerable Miào Jìng explains "only a single moment": as soon as the mental consciousness moves, the eye-consciousness's independent moment is over. The eye never judges good or bad by itself.

The same five headings now apply to hearing. Note the threefold division of sound by cause: sound from **appropriated** elements (執受大種), such as a voice, which comes from a living body; sound from **non-appropriated** elements, such as wind in the trees; and sound from both, such as a stringed instrument played by hand. To "appropriate" (執受, *upādāna*) is the ālayavijñāna's holding of the body as its own, so that it can feel. We shall meet the word again.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, which five items, taken together, are named the Stage Corresponding to the Body of the Five Sense Consciousnesses?
options: attention, contact, feeling, perception, and volition
the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness
mind, thought, consciousness, faculty, and object
the self-nature of the body of the five sense consciousnesses, their support, their object, their accompaniments, and their activity
quiz.why: The treatise opens with exactly this list: "It is the self-nature of the body of the five sense consciousnesses, their support, their object, their accompaniments, and their activity. Taken together, these are named the Stage Corresponding to the Body of the Five Sense Consciousnesses." Option A is the most common confusion: those are the five universal mental factors, which belong *inside* one of the five items (the accompaniments), not the framework itself. B names the five consciousnesses from §2 — what "the body of the five sense consciousnesses" refers to — not the five corresponding factors. C borrows "mind, thought, and consciousness" from the Mind Stage in §16.

quiz.q: The treatise names three supports of the eye-consciousness. Which pairing is correct?
options: the co-existent support is the eye; the immediately-preceding support is the manas; the seed support is the ālayavijñāna
the co-existent support is the manas; the immediately-preceding support is the eye; the seed support is the ālayavijñāna
the co-existent support is form; the immediately-preceding support is attention; the seed support is the four great elements
the co-existent support is the eye; the immediately-preceding support is the seventh consciousness; the seed support is the parents' fluids
quiz.why: "Its support: the co-existent support is the eye. The immediately-preceding support is the manas. The seed support is the ālayavijñāna — the ripening consciousness that holds and carries all seeds." B swaps the first two supports. D contains two traps: the manas here is not the seventh consciousness (see Q2-3), and "seed" here is not the borrowed sense of §40, where it refers to the parents' fluids.

quiz.q: Both Venerable Miào Jìng and Master Cháng Bǎi map the eye-consciousness's three supports onto the four conditions. Which mapping is correct?
options: co-existent support = causal condition; immediately-preceding support = dominant condition; seed support = object condition
co-existent support = dominant condition; immediately-preceding support = immediately-preceding condition; seed support = causal condition
all three supports are object conditions
co-existent support = immediately-preceding condition; immediately-preceding support = causal condition; seed support = dominant condition
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "The co-existent support is the dominant condition … the immediately-preceding condition … the seed support is the causal condition." Master Cháng Bǎi reads it the same way: the eye-faculty stands with the eye-consciousness moment by moment, and if it fails the eye-consciousness cannot arise — the dominant condition; the eye-consciousness of the moment just gone, by ceasing, clears space for the next — the immediately-preceding condition; the seed of eye-consciousness carried in the ālayavijñāna ripening into activity is the causal condition proper. The remaining condition, the object condition, corresponds to the visible form of §7, which is not one of the three supports, so C is wrong.

quiz.q: What image does Venerable Miào Jìng use for "perfuming," and what view does he say Yogācāra therefore does not accept?
options: water wearing through stone; Yogācāra does not accept karma
incense placed in a wooden chest; since perfuming presupposes arising and ceasing, Yogācāra does not accept the Awakening of Faith's teaching that suchness is perfumed
a lamp lighting a dark room; Yogācāra does not accept ignorance
a seed sprouting; Yogācāra does not accept the ālayavijñāna
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng compares perfuming to "incense placed in a wooden chest": at the moment the scent is absorbed it leaves no visible trace, yet it is fully there, ready to surface later as fragrance — just as a moment of grasping leaves no visible trace, yet is stored as a seed, ready to ripen into experience (the Ru-Yi reading note cites the same image). He then points out that only what arises and ceases can be perfumed, "so the principles of the Yogācāra school do not accept the *Awakening of Faith*'s 'suchness receiving perfuming.'" D contradicts itself: perfuming is precisely perfuming into the ālayavijñāna.

quiz.q: The treatise says the form that is the eye-consciousness's object has, "briefly stated," three kinds. What are they?
options: agreeable, disagreeable, and neither
earth, water, fire, and wind
visible and obstructive, invisible and obstructive, invisible and unobstructive
visible colour, shape, and expressive form
quiz.why: "Its object is form — visible, and with obstruction. This again has many kinds. Briefly stated, there are three: visible colour, shape, and expressive form." A is the sixth consciousness's judgement of form as pleasing or not — as Venerable Miào Jìng says, "the eye-consciousness does not make that distinction." B lists the four elements felt by the body-consciousness; C is a general classification of all form by visibility and obstruction, not the three kinds of the eye's object.

quiz.q: Which of the following accords with the treatise's account of the eye-consciousness's activity?
options: it discerns both the particular mark and the shared mark
it discerns the past, the future, and the present
it discerns only the particular mark; it discerns only the present; and it discerns for only a single moment
it initiates, on its own, pure and impure actions of every kind
quiz.why: "It discerns only the particular mark [of its object, not the mark it shares with other things]; it discerns only the present; and it discerns for only a single moment." A, B, and D are all activities of the *mental* consciousness in §19 — discerning both particular and shared marks, the three times, and initiating pure and impure actions — set side by side to show the eye-consciousness's limits. The *Pixunji* notes that the word "only" is there to distinguish it from the mental consciousness, which takes in every object, its own and others'.
